lines.text: Boots are by the fire, they were wringing wet. Kettle's on. Don't start thanking me, I've not sat down yet.

Your animals are in the byre with the door shut and that was done an hour since. One thing, though — a night here is half a season gone, so if you're wanted before the turn, sleep out and keep the days. Room only, or supper as well?
The rooms sway. You'll say you won't sleep.
Built out over the water on the stilts, so they move all night. Man in the end room last week told me flat he'd not shut an eye. He was snoring through the floor by ten.
Day rate. Night's when the market's open — four, five, six, linen — so, the day rate. Now.
Everything's in the rate. Feed, the yard, the rest of it — I don't itemise. The key's on the hook at the stair, second door on the left — seven, eight, nine — second door.
Vent side's warmer and it shakes. Other side's cold and it doesn't.
You're in luck, there's a tub going now. The tubs fill straight off the hot spring. Whatever you've got with you comes out of that water better than it went in, and it costs nobody here a penny.
Shutters stay open. Top and bottom, all night, every room. Rule eleven, and the observatory wrote it.

They had me read all twenty-two out loud before they'd let me sign. Third blanket's in the press if the room goes cold, which it will, because — shutters. Anything you want to say about that, say it up the hill.
Snares and salve. Tonic's behind me and it costs what it costs.

Bait's in the crate by your knee, not sorted, so dig. The cheap sort's cut for a whole kind of animal at once, made of whatever that kind eats. The dear ones are cut for one animal and cost three times the money.
Weighted ones want iron and the smith's had none since spring. Works out cheaper than a base one and a salve on top, when he does have it.
Reed bait, the bundle on the end of the trestle, and it has sat there since the thaw looking at me. There's nothing out on that marsh will look at it but a Reedrick.
And Reedrick come through in the summer. Midsummer on, if you want it exact.
Salve, though. Salve moves — everybody comes off that marsh cut about the hands. Tonic when I've got it in, and I've none this week, because the wet spring does for the lot of it.
Night market. Dusk to dawn, and no, we don't do mornings.
Lamp oil, wicks, tonic, silk by the bolt — evening to you! — silk by the bolt. Master snares, now. Two a year come up here. Well. One. Two sounds the better number.
Come autumn a Gloomoth drops on that rail and the whole market steps round it. There's one there now. It's grazing the moss and hasn't noticed there's a stall under it.
Master snares went when the contract went, and I've none coming. Salve I have, and tonic when the cart brings it, which is not this month.
There's nothing growing on this steppe to cut a proper bait out of. So it's the cheap sort or nothing. It'll fetch a Cragmar as often as an Ashvole.
My prices went up the month next door boarded its windows. Up again the spring after.
Not that tin, that's for the wick. Fill's in the flat tin at the end.
Wispurr bait moves in the winter and not otherwise. It's in the drawer with the master snare. That snare has been in there eighteen months now.
The observatory buys its oil off the lampwright direct and walks past this door to do it. Why they do that I don't ask, and they don't say, and I've stopped wondering about it.
